chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from Muhammad ibn Isma'il, from Ali ibn al-Nu'man, from Ibn Muskān, from 'Abd al-Mu'min, from Jabr, who said:
I asked Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who rents out his house and wine is sold in it. He said: 'Its rent is forbidden (haram).'
199 - Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi 'Umayr, from Ibn Udhaynah, who said:

I wrote to Abu 'Abdillah (peace be upon him) asking him about a man who rents out his ship and his beast of burden from someone who carries wine and pigs in or on them. He said: 'There is no harm (in it).'

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: There is no contradiction between these two narrations for two reasons: The first is that it is permissible that the first narration applies to one who knows that wine is sold in it, so it is not permissible for him to rent the house to one with that description. The second is that it applies to one who rents his beast or ship while he does not know what is carried on it; then when that was carried in it, there was no harm upon him.

The other aspect is that he forbade renting the house to one who sells wine because the sale of wine is forbidden, and he permitted renting the ship in which wine is carried because carrying it is not forbidden, as it is permissible that it be carried to be turned into vinegar. And upon this, there is no contradiction between the two narrations.
ai.seo_question: What is the difference between renting a house for wine sales and renting a ship for wine transport in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi records this ruling in *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* to clarify the distinction between the sale of wine (strictly forbidden) and its mere transport (permissible), a nuance resolved by Al-Hassan ibn al-Salih through the conditions of the renter's knowledge and the specific utility of the vessel. This highlights the Shia jurisprudential principle that *ijarah* (renting) is valid unless the specific use is inherently prohibited, distinguishing between the act of selling and the act of carrying. The ruling underscores the practical application of *urf* (customary understanding) in determining the permissibility of commercial transactions involving impure goods.
